analysis.one_liner: Requires eye doctors to give patients their contact lens prescriptions so they can buy lenses anywhere.
analysis.headline: Passed the House 406-12 on November 19, 2003, cleared the Senate by unanimous consent the next day, and was signed into law on December 6, 2003 — giving contact lens patients the right to take their prescriptions to any seller.
analysis.plain_summary: Before this law, many eye doctors would not hand over contact lens prescriptions — or charged extra fees, required patients to buy lenses from the office, or asked them to sign waivers — so patients had little choice but to buy lenses where they got their exam. The law requires doctors to give every patient a copy of the prescription automatically and for free, and bans those conditions. It sets up a fast verification system so sellers can fill prescriptions: if the doctor does not object within eight business hours, the order goes through. It also bars ads claiming lenses can be bought without a prescription, and puts the FTC in charge of enforcement and a study of competition in lens sales.
analysis.who_benefits: Contact lens wearers — tens of millions of Americans — gain the right to take their prescription to any seller and shop on price, the same freedom eyeglass patients have had under a 1978 FTC rule the bill directs the FTC to review. Internet, mail-order, chain, and discount sellers gain access to those customers through automatic prescription release and the quick verification process.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tens of millions of contact lens wearers

how_it_helps.text: Prescribers must give every patient a copy of the contact lens prescription when the fitting is done, whether or not the patient asks, and cannot charge an extra fee for it.
Doctors cannot require patients to buy lenses from them, pay extra, or sign a liability waiver as a condition of releasing the prescription.

Sellers get a fast verification path: if the prescriber does not respond within eight business hours, the prescription counts as verified and the seller may fill it — so a slow doctor's office cannot stall a rival's sale.
Prescriptions cannot expire in less than a year unless the doctor documents a medical reason in the patient's record, so wearers are not forced into extra exam visits just to keep buying lenses.

Violations are enforced by the FTC as unfair or deceptive practices, and the FTC must report to Congress on competition in lens sales, including exclusive prescriber-manufacturer deals and price differences between online and offline sellers.

analysis.who_pays: Eye care practices lose the captive in-office lens sales, prescription-release fees, and waiver practices the law bans, and must staff prescription verifications and keep records of them. Wearers still bear the cost of an eye exam and prescription renewal at least once a year, since lenses remain prescription-only.
analysis.who_pays_short: Eye care practices selling lenses in-office

drawbacks.text: Contact lenses stay prescription-only, so wearers must keep paying for eye exams and prescription renewals to keep buying. Supporters defend this on eye-health grounds — lenses sit directly on the eye and an outdated fit can damage it — but the bill never considered the cheaper alternative of over-the-counter sale.

A seller can ship lenses after eight business hours even if no doctor ever confirmed the prescription was accurate — silence counts as verification. Speed for shoppers comes at the cost of that confirmation step.

Prescribing offices still hold a lever over rival sellers: within the eight-hour window a doctor can declare the prescription invalid and stop the sale, and every verification contact gives the prescription-holding office a touchpoint with each competitor's order.
Sellers must keep records of every verification communication with prescribers, an administrative cost that falls hardest on small sellers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core gain is real and lands in wallets: a recurring purchase for tens of millions of people became price-competitive, and the eight-business-hour rule stops a silent doctor's office from quietly blocking a sale. The honest costs: every order still routes through the prescriber's office, sellers take on verification and recordkeeping work, and the law leaves lenses prescription-only with renewal at least yearly, so wearers never get the option of buying without an exam — a trade-off supporters defend on eye-health grounds. On balance this was a well-aimed consumer bill: it took the profession's captive retail sales while leaving its gatekeeper role intact.

outcome.mechanism: It swept through in under three months: the House passed it 406-12 on a fast-track vote needing two-thirds, the Senate agreed to it without amendment by unanimous consent the next day, and the President signed it into law on December 6, 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Burr introduced H.R. 3140 on September 23, 2003; the Energy and Commerce subcommittee marked it up the next day, and the full committee ordered it reported amended by voice vote on October 1 and reported it on October 15.
On November 19, 2003, the House passed it 406-12 under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds majority; 197 of 205 Democrats and 208 of 228 Republicans voted yes.
The Senate passed the bill without amendment by unanimous consent on November 20, 2003, with no roll-call vote.
President Bush signed it on December 6, 2003, and it became Public Law 108-164.
The law took effect 60 days after enactment, with the first FTC rules due within 180 days and an FTC competition report to Congress due within 12 months.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Contact lens wearers, who can now shop anywhere for lenses, and the online, mail-order, and chain sellers who gained those customers. Prescribing eye doctors lost the captive in-office lens trade, though the law kept them as the gatekeeper every purchase must pass through.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Contact lens wearers and discount lens sellers

sides.party_line_note: House passage was 406-12, with 197 of 205 Democrats and 208 of 228 Republicans in favor, and the Senate passed it by unanimous consent with no roll-call vote.

industries.note: Eye doctors lose the captive lens trade the law outlaws — mandatory in-office purchases, fees for prescription copies, and liability waivers — but the law locks in their role as the mandatory gatekeeper: no one can buy lenses without a prescription from a prescriber, renewed at least yearly, and every third-party order must be verified through the prescribing office or wait out the eight-hour clock.

industries.industry: Online, mail-order, and chain contact lens sellers
industries.note: Automatic prescription release and the eight-business-hour deemed verification open the retail channel that prescribing offices used to lock up, letting these sellers compete on price for the same prescriptions.

Lens makers gain a larger, fully legal retail market now that any seller can fill prescriptions. Two counterweights: prescriptions for store-brand lenses must name the equivalent national brand, and the FTC must study exclusive manufacturer-prescriber relationships.
